title: The Goldilocks Fallacy: The Undefined Limits of Korea’s Nuclear Role
gist: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee argue that Vipin Narang's 'Goldilocks' framing of South Korea's nuclear options commits a fallacy by collapsing three distinct questions, designation, deployment, and role, onto one scale, which erases the question of South Korea's role in operating U.S. nuclear weapons. They contend Seoul should push for U.S. theater designation and joint targeting to move toward a NATO-style execution role, arguing geography justifies only the form of deployment, not the exclusion of an allied role.

insights.claim: At South Korea's second Deterrence Symposium on July 24, 2026, Vipin Narang argued the 'just right' Goldilocks option for Seoul is strengthening American extended deterrence, ruling out both North Korea's denuclearization (a delusion) and South Korea's own nuclear armament (long-term pain and risk).
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Establishes the U.S. policy anchor the authors are contesting, shaping the terms of the Korea extended-deterrence debate.
insights.quote: the optimal policy for meeting North Korea’s advancing nuclear and missile threat is the Goldilocks choice of strengthening American extended deterrence
insights.locator: Under the title “Goldilocks of the Nuclear Extended Deterrence,”

insights.claim: Narang further ruled out ground-based tactical nuclear redeployment and NATO-style nuclear sharing, offering instead a sea-launched low-yield nuclear cruise missile fired from U.S. Navy submarines that keeps both operation and delivery exclusively in American hands.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: The sea-based preference is the crux the authors read as deliberately excluding any South Korean operational role.
insights.quote: in the Indo-Pacific, Americans — and Americans only — should fire American nuclear weapons
insights.locator: Read into what Narang excluded

insights.claim: The authors argue that the U.S. president's Aug. 16, 2026 description of North Korea as 'unthreatening and respectful' while ordering scaled-back joint exercises sharpens South Korea's assurance problem.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: A U.S. drawdown of joint exercises signals wavering commitment, feeding South Korean proliferation pressure.
insights.quote: “Unthreatening and respectful.” That is how the president of the United States described North Korea on Aug. 16, 2026
insights.locator: “Unthreatening and respectful.”

insights.claim: The authors' core framework separates three distinct questions the Goldilocks metaphor wrongly merges: designation (is the weapon assigned to the Korean theater), deployment (is it on or off the peninsula), and role (does the U.S. or South Korea fire it).
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: The analytic decomposition is the article's central contribution, showing role can be pursued without deployment.
insights.quote: The first is the question of “designation”... Second, the question of “deployment”... Third, the question of “role”
insights.locator: The metaphor presupposes one more thing

insights.claim: The authors argue the real Goldilocks fallacy is not choosing the middle but cramming three different rulers onto one scale, which makes South Korea's nuclear role an appendage of forward deployment that disappears the moment the U.S. declines to deploy.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific logical move that has silently foreclosed debate over South Korea's role.
insights.quote: the question of South Korea’s role disappears before it even needs to be asked
insights.locator: The problem arises when the Goldilocks frame lumps

insights.claim: The authors note Narang keeps designation, deployment, and role separate for Europe in his 2025 Foreign Affairs article with Pranay Vaddi, even placing ground-based options on the table to replace the B61-12, undercutting his merged single-scale approach for Korea.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Uses Narang's own European analysis to expose the inconsistency in his Korea prescription.
insights.quote: Narang keeps these three apart — at least where Europe is concerned
insights.locator: The best evidence for a “no” answer

insights.claim: Narang and Vaddi diagnosed that the Indo-Pacific theater nuclear gap is more serious than Europe's, calling the 'regional nuclear cupboard even more bare' and arguing the 'tyranny of distance' degrades U.S. bombers, making Narang an advocate of nuclear expansion rather than reduction.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Establishes that the disagreement is about role-sharing, not whether to expand nuclear capability.
insights.quote: the United States should develop “more, different, and better” nuclear capabilities and deploy them in new ways
insights.locator: Narang and Vaddi further diagnosed

insights.claim: The authors argue geography can justify only the form of deployment (sea-based for a maritime theater), not the questions of designation and role, since a sea-launched weapon can still be designated to Korean contingencies and involve South Korea in planning and targeting.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Neutralizes the main U.S. justification for excluding South Korea from an operational nuclear role.
insights.quote: geography can serve as an argument that distinguishes the form of deployment. It cannot serve as an argument for excluding the role
insights.locator: Narang justifies this asymmetry based on geography

insights.claim: The authors cite Jennifer Lind and Daryl G. Press's 2026 Foreign Affairs argument that extended deterrence lost credibility after the Cold War because the U.S. faces regional rather than near-existential threats, thinning its incentive to risk nuclear war for an ally.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Grounds South Korean assurance anxiety in a mainstream structural critique of the U.S. nuclear umbrella.
insights.quote: as the United States came to face “regional security challenges, rather than near-existential threats,” its incentive to risk nuclear war for an ally also thinned
insights.locator: Jennifer Lind and Daryl G. Press pointed

insights.claim: The authors treat Lind and Press's appearance in Foreign Affairs, arguing the U.S. should support South Korea's own nuclear armament even outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty, as a signal that excluding tactical nuclear deployment as an extreme option is no longer self-evident.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Mainstreaming of South Korean armament arguments raises the tail risk of Northeast Asian proliferation.
insights.quote: The very fact that such an argument appeared in a mainstream outlet like Foreign Affairs is a signal
insights.locator: Extending this diagnosis

insights.claim: The authors note Elbridge Colby confirmed on Aug. 5, 2026 that his office is reviewing nuclear employment guidance, with his greatest concern being a regional war in which an adversary uses nuclear weapons locally and escalation spreads outward.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Signals an active U.S. shift toward limited-nuclear-use options that could reopen the Korea role question.
insights.quote: the undersecretary of war for policy... confirmed that his office is reviewing nuclear employment guidance
insights.locator: What is happening in Washington right now

insights.claim: The authors define three stages of South Korea's nuclear role, US-alone (already passed), support (conventional forces underwrite U.S. nuclear operations via escort, SEAD, and targeting), and execution (South Korean forces directly operate U.S. nuclear weapons via European-style sharing), and argue Seoul should aim at execution.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Provides the concrete ladder of ambition that defines what a deeper U.S.-ROK nuclear arrangement would look like.
insights.quote: The third and final stage is execution, the stage in which South Korean conventional forces directly operate American nuclear weapons.
insights.locator: In this context, it is worth examining in three stages

insights.claim: The authors argue the 2023 Washington Declaration's codified role for South Korea remains stuck at the support stage, since its 'joint execution and planning' refers only to South Korean conventional support, never to South Korea directly operating American nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Clarifies that current alliance documents fall short of the execution role, framing the policy gap.
insights.quote: The nuclear role the Washington Declaration codified for South Korea remains, in effect, at the second stage: support.
insights.locator: The Washington Declaration of April 26, 2023

insights.claim: The authors argue the same deployment-risk objections (that warheads on Korean soil would be an early target and harder to control in a crisis) were improperly extended to bury the separate question of an execution role, so the alliance never rejected execution on its own merits.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Shows the debate has conflated distinct risks, leaving a legitimate option unexamined.
insights.quote: the disagreement is no longer about risk. It is about who may raise the question at all
insights.locator: There is a reason this codified role has remained hollow

insights.claim: The authors cite NATO's dual-capable aircraft model, in which allied pilots operate American warheads under dual-key procedures, noting the F-35A received B61-12 delivery certification on Oct. 12, 2023 and the Netherlands became the first to formally assign the F-35A to the nuclear strike mission on June 1, 2024.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Provides the concrete European template South Korea's advocates point to as achievable execution.
insights.quote: on June 1, 2024, became the first in the world to formally assign the F-35A to the nuclear strike mission
insights.locator: In fact, the F-35A received B61-12 delivery certification

insights.claim: The authors identify theater designation, whether the U.S. designates a nuclear asset to the Korean theater, as the core determinant separating South Korea from NATO allies, arguing designation is independent of an asset's location and is the precondition for any joint operation or delivery role.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Pinpoints designation as the actionable lever Seoul should demand, ahead of any deployment debate.
insights.quote: one core determinant separating South Korea from the NATO allies is whether the United States has made a theater designation
insights.locator: What, then, lifted Europe to this execution stage

insights.claim: The authors argue Washington's reasons for deferring designation, reduced crisis discretion and signaling commitment to Beijing and Moscow, apply equally to Europe where the U.S. judged the costs worth paying, so the question is why the costs are bearable in one theater and not the other.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Reframes U.S. reluctance as a choice rather than a constraint, strengthening Seoul's case for parity.
insights.quote: why the costs are bearable in one theater and not in another, not whether the costs can be borne at all
insights.locator: Another point deserving attention

insights.claim: The authors identify a deterrence gap where a crisis moves past South Korea's proportionate conventional response but below America's strategic nuclear threshold, precisely where North Korea aims via a low-yield tactical detonation on an uninhabited island or an EMP that would make U.S. strategic retaliation non-credible.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Defines the specific escalation rung that current posture leaves uncovered, the strategic problem driving the whole argument.
insights.quote: what lies immediately above it is only extended deterrence by American strategic nuclear weapons, and the space in between is empty
insights.locator: There is a clear gap in South Korea’s deterrence posture

insights.claim: The authors argue the sea-launched missile is only a temporary second-best rather than an alternative to redeployment, because South Korean forces cannot operate it, an American submarine fires it, so it circumvents the role problem instead of solving it.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the U.S. preferred solution, arguing it leaves South Korea's assurance gap unresolved.
insights.quote: It circumvents the role problem rather than solving it, and so it stands as a temporary second-best
insights.locator: At this point, some experts say the sea-launched missile

insights.claim: The authors argue that because deterrence works only when the adversary perceives capability, an asset's location is not a neutral variable, so the alliance should not rule out ground-based options in advance even while pursuing designation and joint targeting first.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: Keeps ground-based deployment as a live conditional option, hardening the negotiating posture toward Washington.
insights.quote: If visibility is a component of deterrence, then the asset’s location is not an entirely neutral variable.
insights.locator: What is clear is that deterrence does not depend on capability alone

insights.claim: The authors' bottom line is that South Korea should insist on being one of the parties that sets the default in the alliance's nuclear division of labor, rather than passively accepting a boundary Washington draws by rejecting designation, deployment, and execution without sufficient examination.
insights.speaker: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
insights.so_what: States the policy demand that closes the piece, signaling growing Seoul pressure for a codified nuclear role.
insights.quote: A default is not simply given but set by someone. There is no reason South Korea should be left out of that “someone.”
insights.locator: What matters in the end is whether the alliance answers

source_meta.author: Hanbyeol Sohn and Kyung Suk Lee
